Implies a Jewish community at Arbel in Lower Galilee producing a leading sage; Leibner (2009: 254) cautions that the tradition comes from the Mishnah (edited c. 200 CE). No count.

Event: Josephus, War 1.16.2-4 (1.304-313): after taking Sepphoris, Herod sent three cohorts of foot and a troop of horse 'to the village Arbela' (40 days later a pitched battle with supporters of Antigonus, whose right wing routed Herod's left wing before Herod won); afterwards Herod's men, let down in chests from the cliff, 'slew the robbers and their families' in the caves near the village. Dated c. 39-38 BCE (Leibner). Attests a Jewish (pro-Hasmonean) population in and around Arbel. Josephus gives no count of inhabitants; Leibner (citing Shatzman) puts Herod's force at 5,000-7,000 troops and Antigonus' supporters at several thousand soldiers - army sizes, not residents, so Population blank.

Event: Josephus, Life 37 (188): at the outbreak of the Great Revolt Josephus, as commander in Galilee, fortified among the villages of Lower Galilee 'the cave of Arbela' and stored grain and arms there (parallel War 2.20.6 (2.573): walls about the caves near the lake of Gennesar). Dated 66 CE. No count.

Literary presence: Josephus, Life 60 (311): 'I came to the village Arbela, where I procured an assembly of the Galileans' to hear the envoys denounce Jonathan's delegation from Jerusalem (c. winter 66/67 CE). Leibner reads this as showing that Arbel supported Josephus and the revolt. Attests an inhabited Jewish village used as Josephus' rallying point; no count.

Archaeological presence: Shivtiel's survey of the cliff shelters on Mount Arbel (over 300 caves used as shelters on Arbel-Nitai; about 35 plastered cisterns and 5 caves with hewn ritual baths (miqvaot) on Mount Arbel; early Roman pottery in rope-access shelters; coins of John Hyrcanus I and Alexander Jannaeus) links them to the Jews of the settlement of Arbel, who prepared them as refuges, apparently in the Great Revolt (Galilee campaign 67 CE, c.; Josephus fortified the 'Arbel caves'). Evidence of an observant Jewish population; no count.
